reasoning: The prompt asks 'what do I ACTUALLY cut' — a request for a decision, not a procedure for reaching one. A answers it: it identifies the specific 915-line file, audits it section by section, and returns a line-numbered cut list with destinations (915 -> ~142, -85%). I independently re-ran the numbers against the file A names: every structural claim checks out — competency definitions at 34-131, anti-patterns at 132-140, Steps 1-5 at 255-420, Steps 6-7 at 421-508, Step 8 at 509-752, examples at 771-850, pitfalls at 851-897. A's 'about 195 of 243 lines dead per run' for Step 8 is right too: the five mutually-exclusive branches total 238 lines and the largest is 72, so 166-201 lines never fire on a given session. B answers a different, adjacent question: how to find out what to cut. Its Step 1 audit commands are real and run correctly, but they output a heading map, not a decision, and every yield figure in its cut list is labelled 'typical for a 900-line file'. The reader finishes B still owing themselves the work. Beyond groundedness, three things separate them. (1) A has a fourth destination B lacks: deterministic prose -> scripts/. B's item #2 only relocates code that is already code; A converts 88 lines of prose arithmetic and if/else rules into scripts/score.py, and repurposes the three worked examples from context cost into test fixtures for it. That is a categorically better move, and it is the kind of thing only a section-by-section read surfaces. (2) A reads the frontmatter, finds disable-model-invocation: true, and uses it to argue against splitting into separate skills — the cost is the user's memory, not the context window. I confirmed that flag is present. B assumes automatic invocation and closes by floating exactly the split A rules out, so on this file B's final recommendation is wrong for a reason A names. (3) A's verification is stronger where it counts: check 5 runs the same five answers against old and new and requires the recommended priority and delivered plan to be identical — a behavioural-equivalence test on the actual decision output, versus B's looser 'diff the behaviour'. B is not weak, and it wins real points. Its 'what does not get cut' section is the best original passage in either document: compressing the method into the description field as the highest-damage available move, rationalization tables being load-bearing precisely because they look repetitive, explicit no-exception clauses being the belt rather than belt-and-braces. A has no equivalent to the description-field trap. B also contributes durable general rules A misses — keep every reference one level deep, add a contents list to any split file over 100 lines, avoid @-style auto-loading links that force-load the target — and better statistics (5 runs for wording-sensitive checks, spread treated as data, versus A's 3/3). B is the better general method and would transfer to a file A's specifics cannot touch. But B's own transferability is undercut when its audit meets this file: running B's command 2 returns '11 of 915 lines (1%) inside 1 blocks', and B's own stress test says that under ~25% code+reference it should 'throw out this ordering and treat it as an editing job'. That verdict is wrong here — the real win is a relocation win (one branch of five fires per run), which B's Step 2 classification would catch but its Step 3 cut list, dominated by code, language-variant examples and flowcharts this file does not have, does not name. B's calibration is also invented (200-300 target, 500 ceiling) where A's is measured against the corpus the file lives in (n=141, median 134, p75 301), which I verified. All four expectations pass for both outputs, so they do not discriminate; the rubric does. A wins on groundedness, diagnostic correctness and the sharper sorting principle (its reason-vs-recite test — 'needed every run' and 'needed in context from turn one' are different claims — is the single best idea in either document and is what unlocks the rubric relocation). B wins on transferability and on naming failure modes A missed. On a question whose operative word is 'actually', the answer beats the method.

strengths: Identifies the actual file and audits it section by section; every line-number claim I re-checked is correct (34-131, 132-140, 255-420, 421-508, 509-752, 771-850, 851-897)
Reason-vs-recite test is the sharpest principle in either document: 'needed every run' and 'needed in context from turn one' are different claims, and it is what licenses moving the maturity rubric
Four destinations, not three: adds deterministic-prose -> scripts/, converting 88 lines of arithmetic and if/else rules into scripts/score.py
Repurposes the three worked examples from context cost into test fixtures for that script — same content, changed role
Reads the frontmatter, finds disable-model-invocation: true (confirmed), and correctly argues the split-into-skills move is worse here because the cost is the user's memory
Ordering has a stated dependency rationale — never relocate what you were going to delete, never disclose a duplicate into two files — not just risk-ranking
Repo-calibrated target (n=141, median 134, p75 301) instead of an invented budget
Verification check 5 is a true behavioural-equivalence test: same five answers, old vs new, priority and plan must be identical
Pointer-wording section gives a weak/strong contrast and the right triage rule: fix the wording before pulling material back inline

Stress test is genuinely self-critical — names the file inference as the weakest link, and identifies verbatim-rubric drift as a consistency regression introduced by a readability fix, with a stated fallback (300 lines that work beat 142 that drift)
weaknesses: Stakes the specifics on inferring the file from a line count; if wrong, every line number evaporates (it says so)
Less useful as a reusable method than B — the sorting rule transfers, the cut list does not
Does the measurement for the reader rather than teaching them to measure, so nothing is learned for the next file
The ~142 'after' figure is a projection that cannot be checked until the work is done
Misses the description-field compression trap and the one-level-deep / auto-loading-link rules that B names

strengths: States the reframe most crisply in the opening line — length is not the defect, unreachability is — with a good pricing analogy (content needed 10% of the time priced as if needed 100%)
Decision layer vs execution layer is a memorable and correct dividing line, and its Step 2 classification question ('only for one branch of the work?') does catch the biggest real win
Audit commands are real and run correctly as written; the awk fence-tracking so code comments are not counted as headings is a careful touch

'What does not get cut' is the best original passage in either document — description-field compression as the highest-damage move, rationalization tables load-bearing precisely because they look repetitive, no-exception clauses as the belt
Durable general rules A lacks: keep references one level deep, contents list on any split file over 100 lines, avoid @-style auto-loading links
Better statistics than A: 5 runs for wording-sensitive checks, and spread across runs treated as data in its own right
Opens by telling the user to ask the two readers WHERE they bounced, not whether it is long — a genuinely good move on a vague complaint
90-minute timeboxed plan with a before-cut baseline, and a three-way reading of the behaviour diff that correctly distinguishes a broken pointer from load-bearing content
weaknesses: Answers 'how do I find out what to cut' when the question was 'what do I actually cut' — the reader finishes still owing themselves the audit
Every yield figure is 'typical for a 900-line file'; no number is a measurement
Assumes automatic invocation, which is wrong for this file, and the error propagates into the closing recommendation to split into separate skills — precisely the move that is wrong here

Its own audit invalidates much of its cut list on this file: command 2 returns 1% of lines inside code blocks, and items 1, 2, 3 and 6 lean on code, language-variant examples and flowcharts that are not present
Its stress-test escape hatch ('under ~25% code+reference, treat it as an editing job') would send the reader the wrong way here, since the real win is branch-based relocation
Budget is invented rather than calibrated; a 500-line ceiling would bless a file well above the corpus 75th percentile
The section-allocation table (80-120 lines for the core procedure) is generic scaffolding that does little work
No equivalent of A's deterministic-prose-to-script tier — item 2 only relocates code that is already code
